[18] Moreover, I have the jurisdiction to conduct an independent assessment and, therefore, can clarify on appeal that this case is not being determined on the basis of credibility. While I do find credibility concerns on the record, these would constitute new issues, and therefore I am not relying upon them. For the purposes of the appeal, I accept the credibility of the Appellant's testimony in-so-much as credibility is taken to mean that the Appellant is not lying or being deceptive.

[19] In discussing credibility in this case, I find it important to review the framework for analysis of evidence set out by Justice Grammond in Magonza as this is at the heart of the claim.7 Justice Grammond sets out what he calls "basic concepts" in making findings of fact, including: credibility, probative value, weight and sufficiency. These are crucial to understanding the issues in this claim. To summarize, they are as follows:
(a) Credibility: made up of the trustworthiness or honesty of the evidence and the reliability in terms of the witnesses' ability to recall or recount the facts. Assessing credibility involves a number of factors, including: observation, memory, consistency, corroboration, plausibility, bias and demeanour.8
(b) Probative value: the capacity or degree to which the evidence establishes the question at hand.9
(c) Weight: how persuasive the evidence is, based upon the credibility and probative value.10
(d) Sufficiency: a decision as to whether the cumulative weight of the evidence is sufficient to reach a conclusion.11

[20] This case is not about credibility, in terms of the honesty of the Appellant. The RPD concluded that the Appellant honestly believes that the problems he has encountered (death of his child, motor vehicle accident) are caused by the Ogboni cult. Rather, this is a question of probative value, weight and sufficiency. The RPD assessed these concepts indirectly. For example, the RPD noted that there was no direct evidence that the Ogboni cult had committed the harms alleged. They were not present at the death of the child or the accident. They did not directly reference these things in any telephone calls. In my view, these factors diminish the probative value of the Appellant's testimony in which he believes that the accident and death of his child are caused by the Ogboni.

[21] The Appellant argues that it was an error for the RPD to not make a negative credibility finding and then give no weight to the Appellant's claim.12 This confuses the concepts above. Credibility of a statement does not automatically mean it is given weight. The Appellant argues that the RPD did not consider the testimony about the threatening phone calls. I disagree. The RPD specifically references the phone calls and state that the calls contained "ambiguous messages that do not make a direct reference to the accident."13 Reviewing the record, I agree with this assessment of the calls. The Appellant testified that he was called and told, "wherever you went, you still come to a point" and that they would say "[o]h is that you Adewale," and he knew it was members of the Ogboni.14

[22] Specifically, when asked about the motor accident, he said the following:
PERSON CONCERNED: I, I had a dream during that period when I was asleep. The second day, when I (indiscernible), that was the -- the accident happened. Even while I'm here, somebody will just call on the phone and threaten, making threatening statements (indiscernible) my changing the phone number five times.15

[23] I agree that these are generic threats which do not connect to the alleged harms, and therefore they have low probative value.

For example, in the case cited by the Appellant, there was evidence accepted that the Ogboni cult invaded the home of the persons concerned and violently assaulted and threatened them.25 These facts are not similar to this case. That case did not centre on the ability of the Ogboni to use spiritual powers to harm someone.

[33] The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to "offer a culturally appropriate analysis" of the claim.26 I disagree. In my view, the RPD was particularly sensitive to the fact that the Appellant comes from a different culture and may have different beliefs. The RPD did not find it lacked credibility that the Appellant believed he was being targeted through supernatural means. REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] I dismiss the appeal of XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria.

[2] The Appellant alleges that his father was a member of the Ogboni cult and that in 1994, one year after his father's death, he was approached by the Ogboni who said that his father's position had been transferred to the Appellant. The Appellant alleges that he was told that he had seven days and seven nights to take the position or vacate the land he had inherited from his father. The Appellant alleges that he declined. XXXX XXXX later, his daughter died, and the Appellant believes this was caused by voodoo from the Ogboni cult. The Appellant relocated to Osun state, and he alleges that he continued to have nightmares, threatening phone calls and that he was in a motor vehicle accident that he believes was caused by the Ogboni's powers.

[3] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejected the claim finding that there was no objective basis for the claim that the Appellant has a forward-facing risk. The RPD considered that there was no objective evidence that the death of the child or the accident was caused by the Ogboni and that the only other problems were phone calls, and there were no personal confrontations. Therefore, the RPD concluded that the Appellant did not have a risk.

[4] The Appellant argues that the RPD erred. He argues that his testimony was credible and that the RPD erred by saying the decision was one of credibility. He argues that the RPD erred in concluding that there was no objective risk, that it failed to consider the country documents and did not use an appropriate cultural lens to assess the claim. The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred by failing to assess whether the claim fell under section 96 or 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA). The Appellant submits one new piece of evidence and has not requested a hearing.

[5] I find that the RPD's ultimate conclusion is correct. I agree with the Appellant that the RPD could have more clearly articulated the nexus to the Convention and improperly found forward-facing risk to be part of credibility. However, these issues are not determinative. The Appellant has not established a serious possibility of persecution or section 97(1) risk on a forward-facing basis.
DECISION

[6] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
NEW EVIDENCE
The evidence presented by the Appellant is rejected

[7] According to the law,1 I can only accept evidence that:
(i) arose after the RPD's decision; or
(ii) was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
(iii) that the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
[8] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.2

[9] The Appellant submits one academic article, "Adjudicating Fear of Witchcraft Claims in Refugee Law," as new evidence.3 The Appellant acknowledges that the article does not post-date the rejection of the claim and was available at the time of the hearing. The Appellant argues that he could not reasonably have been expected to provide this evidence prior to the rejection of the claim because he "could not have reasonably be[en] expected to justify by doctrine his fear of witchcraft, whereas the jurisprudence from this tribunal and the country conditions were abundant on the matter."4 I disagree.

[10] The Appellant had Counsel before the RPD who was aware that the allegations involved a spiritual nature and could have submitted this article to the RPD before the hearing. Moreover, the RPD repeatedly asked the Appellant if he had any reason to believe that there was any evidence of a connection between the incidents of fear and the Ogboni cult. The RPD put the issue squarely to the Appellant at the hearing. The Appellant did not ask for an opportunity to put forward further evidence about witchcraft claims. Almost one month passed from the point of the hearing to the decision, and the Appellant made no effort to submit post-hearing documents. I therefore find the Appellant has not established that he could not reasonably have been expected to provide this document prior to the rejection of his claim. I find that the Appellant is attempting to use the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to supplement the record before the RPD, which is not permissible. I therefore reject the article.
[11] The Appellant did not request an oral hearing, and given that I have not accepted any new evidence, I cannot convene one.
ANALYSIS

[12] My role is to look at all of the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.5 There is an exception to this, where the RAD defers to the RPD if the RPD had a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility of oral evidence. I do not find this case falls into the exception. Therefore, I will be looking at whether the RPD's decision was correct.

[13] In this case, while I find that there are some errors in the decision, I find that the ultimate conclusion is correct, and I confirm the decision of the RPD.
Nexus

[14] The Appellant argues that the RPD's decision is not transparent and justifiable because there is no separate analysis under section 96 or 97 which leads to confusing in understanding the decision. I agree that the RPD did not clearly identify the nexus, but I find this has no bearing on the outcome of the decision.

[15] The Appellant alleged that he refused the chief position because he is Christian, and he felt the group was contrary to his religious beliefs.6 Therefore, this claim has a nexus to the Convention. The RPD identified this by assessing whether there was a serious possibility of persecution but did not clearly state the nexus. I do not find this to be a determinative error. Moreover, as I will explain below, I find the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant had not established a serious possibility of persecution. For the same reasons, I find that the Appellant has not established a section 97(1) risk, on a balance of probabilities, which has a higher standard of proof than a claim under section 96.
Credibility

[16] The Appellant argues, first, that the RPD found him to be a credible witness and, second, that the RPD erred by framing the decision as one of credibility. I agree that the RPD improperly confused headings of credibility and objective risk, but I do not find this error determinative. I also find that the RPD generally accepted that the Appellant's testimony was credible, but I do not find that this necessitates allowing this claim, as I will explain below.

[17] With regard to the categorization of the claim, the RPD held that there was no objective basis for the claim on a forward-facing basis but used headings in the decision relating to credibility. I agree with the Appellant that this was an error. However, I find it has no impact on the decision because the RPD made clear that the Appellant's beliefs were found to be credibly held and that this was a decision relating to objective risk and forward-facing risk.

[18] Moreover, I have the jurisdiction to conduct an independent assessment and, therefore, can clarify on appeal that this case is not being determined on the basis of credibility. While I do find credibility concerns on the record, these would constitute new issues, and therefore I am not relying upon them. For the purposes of the appeal, I accept the credibility of the Appellant's testimony in-so-much as credibility is taken to mean that the Appellant is not lying or being deceptive.

[19] In discussing credibility in this case, I find it important to review the framework for analysis of evidence set out by Justice Grammond in Magonza as this is at the heart of the claim.7 Justice Grammond sets out what he calls "basic concepts" in making findings of fact, including: credibility, probative value, weight and sufficiency. These are crucial to understanding the issues in this claim. To summarize, they are as follows:
(a) Credibility: made up of the trustworthiness or honesty of the evidence and the reliability in terms of the witnesses' ability to recall or recount the facts. Assessing credibility involves a number of factors, including: observation, memory, consistency, corroboration, plausibility, bias and demeanour.8
(b) Probative value: the capacity or degree to which the evidence establishes the question at hand.9
(c) Weight: how persuasive the evidence is, based upon the credibility and probative value.10
(d) Sufficiency: a decision as to whether the cumulative weight of the evidence is sufficient to reach a conclusion.11

[20] This case is not about credibility, in terms of the honesty of the Appellant. The RPD concluded that the Appellant honestly believes that the problems he has encountered (death of his child, motor vehicle accident) are caused by the Ogboni cult. Rather, this is a question of probative value, weight and sufficiency. The RPD assessed these concepts indirectly. For example, the RPD noted that there was no direct evidence that the Ogboni cult had committed the harms alleged. They were not present at the death of the child or the accident. They did not directly reference these things in any telephone calls. In my view, these factors diminish the probative value of the Appellant's testimony in which he believes that the accident and death of his child are caused by the Ogboni.

[21] The Appellant argues that it was an error for the RPD to not make a negative credibility finding and then give no weight to the Appellant's claim.12 This confuses the concepts above. Credibility of a statement does not automatically mean it is given weight. The Appellant argues that the RPD did not consider the testimony about the threatening phone calls. I disagree. The RPD specifically references the phone calls and state that the calls contained "ambiguous messages that do not make a direct reference to the accident."13 Reviewing the record, I agree with this assessment of the calls. The Appellant testified that he was called and told, "wherever you went, you still come to a point" and that they would say "[o]h is that you Adewale," and he knew it was members of the Ogboni.14

[22] Specifically, when asked about the motor accident, he said the following:
PERSON CONCERNED: I, I had a dream during that period when I was asleep. The second day, when I (indiscernible), that was the -- the accident happened. Even while I'm here, somebody will just call on the phone and threaten, making threatening statements (indiscernible) my changing the phone number five times.15
[23] I agree that these are generic threats which do not connect to the alleged harms, and therefore they have low probative value.

[24] The Appellant also argues that the RPD erred because it made no negative credibility findings and yet gave little probative value to the documentary evidence. Again, I find this confuses the concepts of credibility and probative value. The RPD noted that the Appellant had a declaration from his wife and friend. The RPD held that the wife's declaration relates to obtaining documentary evidence (death certificates) and does not speak to the Ogboni cult. Reviewing the record, this is correct. The RPD also held that the friend's affidavit does not provide any information about the cause of the child's death and therefore is insufficient to show an objective basis.16 The affidavit states "his refusal to join the fraternity exposed him to a lot of dangers which included loss of properties, business and of course a child."17 There is no information about how the friend knows this or why he believes these losses relate to the Ogboni. I agree that they do not establish an objective basis when taken together with the Appellant's testimony. They are not particularly probative documents because they have a limited capacity to prove the question at hand which is whether the Ogboni is responsible for the Appellant's misfortunes.

[25] Another way to consider this issue is in terms of speculation. Findings of fact cannot be made based on speculation.18 There is a distinction between something which a witness has direct personal knowledge of and speculation based upon that knowledge.19 The Appellant's direct knowledge is that his child died, and he had a motor vehicle accident. He has knowledge that he received general threats. It is speculation to connect these two things and to connect the death and accident to the Ogboni cult. Even if I were to accept that the Ogboni cult has spiritual powers, which has not been established on the evidence, it is still speculative to conclude that these powers were the cause of the Appellant's child's death and the motor vehicle accident. Speculation is not entitled to evidentiary weight.

[26] I find that the RPD's conclusion that the Appellant is telling the truth does not necessarily amount to a finding that the claim is objectively well founded. I find the RPD's conclusion is correct.
The RPD correctly concluded that the Appellant had not established an objectively well-founded forward-facing risk

[27] The RPD found that, even accepting the Appellant's belief that the harms alleged were connected to the Ogboni cult, this was not established on the evidence, and there was no objective basis for the claim. I agree with this and find it to be correct.

[28] The Appellant argues that the objective documents support the Appellant's risk and that there are examples of the RAD granting protection to individuals who fear the Ogboni. I do not find the objective documents support a finding of risk for the Appellant, and I find the RAD decision the Appellant points to is distinguishable.

[29] The Appellant references two Response to Information Requests (RIRs) in the National Documentation Package (NDP). The first relates to the Ogboni society. The Appellant argues that this document shows that the Ogboni cult has "been known to practice violent supernatural actions".20 I do not agree. The report, as quoted by the Appellant, states:
The Professor of Yoruba studies also commented that the cultural belief in the supernatural cuts across all spheres of life in Yorubaland, even among nominal Christians and Muslims, and "especially" among "traditional religious practitioners" (Professor 27 Mar. 2019). Without providing further details, the Canadian official noted that there is a belief among non-members that the Ogboni society engages in "supernatural" rituals and practices that can be "brutal and violent" (Canada 27 Mar. 2019a). Sources indicate that Ogboni society is alleged to engage in activities such as ritual human sacrifices [or sacrifices involving body parts (Canada 27 Mar. 2019a)] (Sociologist 29 Mar. 2019; Professor 27 Mar. 2019) or blood rituals, or rituals aiming to become wealthy (Professor 27 Mar. 2019)....21

[30] The report notes that it is individuals outside of the group that believe that the group has supernatural powers. This does not provide a strong degree of proof to the question of whether the group actually does have such powers. Moreover, the report notes that the activities alleged include human sacrifice, blood rituals and rituals aiming to become wealthy. There is no mention of any allegations that they can kill people from afar or cause motor vehicle accidents. Moreover, the same article notes that the power of the group is "waning" and has no power or influence remaining.22 The report goes on to state that there is a possibility that a child of a member who refuses to join could face harassment to the point of death, but there is no mention of use of supernatural powers to kill people.23 There are examples of news articles alleging kidnapping and abuse by the Ogboni, but there is no evidence of that here. I therefore find that this RIR does not have a high probative value in establishing a risk to the Appellant.

[31] The second RIR cited by the Appellant indicates there is mixed evidence on whether there are consequences for refusing to take a hereditary chieftaincy position.24 It is not clear that joining the Ogboni is the same as this, and therefore I do not find this article particularly relevant. I generally agree that there can be consequences for refusing a hereditary chieftaincy position, or Ogboni membership, but I do not find that the Appellant has established that he has or would face persecutory consequences in his case for his refusal to join the Ogboni.

[32] As for the RAD's decision cited by the Appellant, I find it is distinguishable. For example, in the case cited by the Appellant, there was evidence accepted that the Ogboni cult invaded the home of the persons concerned and violently assaulted and threatened them.25 These facts are not similar to this case. That case did not centre on the ability of the Ogboni to use spiritual powers to harm someone.

[33] The Appellant argues that the RPD failed to "offer a culturally appropriate analysis" of the claim.26 I disagree. In my view, the RPD was particularly sensitive to the fact that the Appellant comes from a different culture and may have different beliefs. The RPD did not find it lacked credibility that the Appellant believed he was being targeted through supernatural means. The RPD did not show closemindedness as argued but, rather, asked questions to understand the facts in this case. The Appellant argues that there should be no need for any corroboration because as "a Nigerian man [the Appellant] believes that the Ogboni cult members have these supernatural powers to harm and kill."27 I disagree. Cultural sensitivity does not require the RPD to accept that everything the Appellant believes is objectively true but, rather, that the RPD assesses the evidence and draws conclusions based upon it giving clear reasoning based on documentary evidence and logic.

[34] This was the approach set out by my colleague in a decision cited by the Appellant. In that decision, the RAD returned the matter to the RPD because the RPD had ignored important evidence.28 This was also the situation in the second case relating to witchcraft cited by the Appellant.29 I do not find the RPD ignored relevant evidence in this case. As discussed above, the RPD correctly considered the affidavits submitted.

[35] As for the final RAD case cited by the Appellant, I find it is not particularly persuasive given its age, as it was decided prior to the accepted standard of review set out in Huruglica.30 Moreover, in that case, the RPD failed to consider the accepted threats and whether they amounted to persecution, which I find the RPD did in this case. In any event, jurisprudence from the RAD is not binding upon me, and every RAD decision is fact specific.

[36] The facts of this case are distinct from those cited by the Appellant. Significantly, in this case, the threat against the Appellant was that he either take the position his father held "or vacate the land which had become a shrine space."31 The Appellant vacated the land when he moved from Lagos state to Osun state in 1994. Therefore, he has acquiesced to the demands of the Ogboni. He lived in Osun state from 1994 to 2014. He did not encounter anyone from Ogboni personally in that time. He received threatening phone calls, the content of which from his testimony was vague. He was in a motor vehicle accident, which is not mentioned in his amended Basis of Claim form (BOC) and which he did not provide any evidence about when it occurred or medical evidence relating to it, and which he believes was caused by the Ogboni.

[37] The fact that the Appellant gave the Ogboni the land indicates that they have less motive to want to harm him. When I combine this with the low probative value of the Appellant's belief that the accident and death were caused by the Ogboni, I find that there is insufficient evidence to establish a serious possibility of persecution or a section 97(1) risk, on a balance of probabilities, on a forward-facing basis, should the Appellant return to Nigeria. I find that the telephone threats do not constitute persecution nor do they demonstrate a risk of future persecution.
Other grounds of risk

[38] At the RPD hearing, the Appellant also alleged that he feared returning to Nigeria because of the socio-economic and political conditions, including killings. The RPD found that this was a generalized risk. The Appellant has not challenged this on appeal. Reviewing the record, I agree with this conclusion and find it to be correct.
CONCLUSION

[39] I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
